summary: This informational RFC is part of a series on using modern cryptographic mechanisms for message authentication in routing protocols (KARP). It defines a framework for a key management protocol that could create and manage session keys for authentication and integrity.

plainLanguage.summary: Routing protocols need ways to verify messages between routers and replace keys safely. This RFC gives design teams a two-phase plan for improving that protection.

questions: keying and authentication for routing protocols
why use a key management protocol for routers
subtitle: A roadmap for stronger message authentication and key management in routing protocols

tldr.problem: Routing protocols need to protect messages exchanged between peers. Existing approaches often rely on manual keys and may lack modern algorithms, easy rekeying or replay protection.
tldr.mechanism: KARP groups protocols by message and keying patterns, then proposes two phases: improve authentication using existing key management, followed by automated key management.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC provides design guidelines and a work plan. It does not specify a key management protocol or modify any routing protocol.

facts.label: Initial keying phase
facts.value: Modern authentication with existing key management

today: RFC 6518 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a KARP design-guidelines document, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Scope: Protecting Routing Messages
sections.content:
The KARP work addresses protection of routing-protocol packets exchanged between directly communicating peers. It does not address whether routing information is authorized to come from a particular source; that is handled by other mechanisms.

The RFC introduces a conceptual key table between routing protocols, operators and automated key management. A routing protocol can look up the key used for a message, while key-management functions make keys available through the table. This abstraction supports standardization and management; implementations are not required to use it internally.
sections.plainLanguage: This work is about protecting messages that routers exchange with their neighbors. It proposes a shared way for protocols and key-management systems to provide the keys they need.

sections.title: Protocol Message and Keying Categories
sections.content:
The RFC groups protocols by message transaction: one-to-one messages between peers, one-to-many messages on a link, and multicast. It separately groups keying as peer keying, which establishes a security association between two routers, or group keying, which distributes one keying message for use by multiple peers.

These categories help design teams consider whether authentication mechanisms can be shared across protocols. A future key management protocol might serve one or more categories, but the RFC specifies no such protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routing messages go to one neighbor, some to many neighbors and some use multicast. The way keys are shared depends on that communication pattern.

sections.title: Keys, Lifetimes and Rekeying
sections.content:
Designers of manually keyed authentication should consider how a future key management protocol would supply keys, algorithms, key lifetimes, direction and security-association identifiers. Keys should have limited lifetimes, and routers need to change keys without forcing routing sessions or adjacencies to restart.

The RFC discusses asymmetric keys generated and retained on routers as one possible way to prove machine identity. It also cautions that frequent manual key changes can increase exposure if the change process is poorly controlled. A key chain alone does not solve the problem if the routing stack cannot move between keys without disruption.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to change keys without interrupting routing. Automating key changes can reduce manual work, but the protocol first needs to support rekeying safely.

sections.title: The Two-Phase Design Roadmap
sections.content:
Phase 1 updates each routing protocol's authentication to use modern algorithms and key agility within its existing key-management framework. It explicitly excludes creating or embedding a key management protocol. Teams assess the protocol, define a target security state, identify gaps, plan deployment and specify work.

Phase 2 develops automated key management for unique pair-wise keys, or group keys where needed. A KMP can negotiate algorithms and lifetimes, provide fresh session keys, and rekey before keys expire without administrator action. The KMP should remain separate from the routing transport, which uses the resulting security parameters without needing to know how the keys were derived.
sections.plainLanguage: First, improve each protocol's authentication while keeping its current key-management approach. Then add automated key management that can create and replace keys without interrupting routing.

sections.title: Deployment, Denial of Service and Design Checks
sections.content:
New authentication must support incremental deployment and backward compatibility in networks where upgraded and older routers coexist. Designers must also avoid creating denial-of-service opportunities through expensive cryptographic checks, repeated attempts with multiple keys, or state allocated before a peer is verified.

The gap analysis asks each protocol team to consider strong algorithms, algorithm agility, rekeying without disruption, replay protection, processing cost and the requirements of its own protocol. The RFC recommends unpredictable keys and different peer keys where practical; when manual pre-shared keys are used, connection-specific material can be combined through a key-derivation function.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers may be upgraded at different times, so new security needs to work during a transition. Authentication must also avoid giving attackers a cheap way to overload a router.
